deep.reconstruction:
The page is a printed page (p. 56) of a German arithmetic textbook, Leiste's, with handwritten notes by Gauss in the right margin.

PRINTED TEXT

(A) End of example 4 from p. 55 (Gesellschaftsrechnung, i.e. proportional division). Village A must pay 2000 rthl. It has 6 Ackerleute, 6 Halbspänner and 12 Kothsassen, whose individual contributions are in the ratio 1 : 2/3 : 1/2.
- The group weights are a = 6·1 = 6, b = 6·(2/3) = 4, c = 12·(1/2) = 6, so a + b + c = 16.
- All Ackerleute together pay 2000·6/16 = 750, so one Ackermann pays 2000/16 = 125 rthl.
- One Kothsasse pays half of that, 62½ rthl.
- All Halbspänner together pay 2000·4/16 = 500, so one pays 2000·4/(16·6) = 83⅓ rthl.

(B) Example 5: mean price of a mixture.
- Ingredients: 2 Anker of French wine at 5 rthl each, 1 Anker at 8½ rthl, and 1/8 Anker of brandy costing 1 rthl.
- Total volume is 3⅛ = 25/8 Anker; total cost is 10 + 8½ + 1 = 19½ rthl.
- Price per Anker = 19.5/(25/8) = 156/25 = 6.24 rthl. The book calls this 'a mere division example'.

(C) Example 6: alligation (Vermischungs- oder Alligationsrechnung). Given:
- a = price of a quantity q of the dearer good;
- b = price of a quantity q of the cheaper good;
- c = required price of a quantity q of the mixture.
Find x, the amount of the dearer good, with q − x of the cheaper.
- By proportion, the dearer part costs ax/q and the cheaper part costs b(q − x)/q.
- Setting the sum equal to c: c = (ax + bq − bx)/q, so qc − bq = (a − b)x.
- Hence x = (c − b)q/(a − b).

Example: a = 12, b = 8, c = 9, q = 1 gives x = 1/4 Anker and q − x = 3/4. (Check, mine: 12·¼ + 8·¾ = 9.)

The text then starts applying this to silver of different fineness: 15-löthig and 10-löthig silver, with 1 Mark = 16 Loth. It continues on the next page.

GAUSS'S MARGINAL NOTES

(1) A column of ten numbers: 9929, 9857, 9833, 9817, 9769, 9721, 9697, 9689, 9649, 9601.
- My check: all ten are prime and all are ≡ 1 (mod 8).
- They are exactly the ten largest primes ≡ 1 (mod 8) below 10000, listed in descending order.
- Under a rule Gauss writes 97562. This is their sum (computed by me), and 97562/10 = 9756.2, which is the mean Gauss records on the next page.
- The next page repeats this column next to three others headed 9973, 9931 and 9967. These are the last ten primes below 10000 in the classes 5, 3 and 7 mod 8, with means 9788.2, 9849.4 and 9789.4.
- So Gauss is comparing how the primes just below 10^4 fall into the four residue classes mod 8, using the mean of the last ten primes in each class.

(2) Beside the first six primes stand the numbers 152, 60, 104, 48, 52, 92. Their meaning is not determined from this page.
- They are not prime gaps.
- They cannot be the legs of p = a² + b², since 152 > √9929.
- They may be some auxiliary invariant, such as a residue index or a primitive-root-related quantity (unsure).

(3) A short column '20.44 / 40.102 / 60.166' (the last digit of 44 is possibly overwritten). This is also repeated on the next page; its meaning is unclear.

(4) Bottom margin: '6,7 ½' and '2680'. These connect to the computations on the next page, which involve 0.8535533912 and 0.8408964152 in an arithmetic–geometric-mean-type scheme. That scheme is not on this page.
errors: No arithmetic errors in the printed text: 125, 62½, 83⅓, 156/25 and x = (c−b)q/(a−b) = 1/4 are all correct.

Minor exposition point: in example 5 the '1/8 Brantwein zu 1 rthl' means 1/8 Anker costing 1 rthl in total, which is needed for the total of 19½ rthl. The wording is slightly ambiguous but the arithmetic is consistent.
The alligation derivation implicitly assumes b < c < a so that 0 < x < q; this is not stated.

results.what: Mean price of a mixture as total cost divided by total quantity
Alligation formula x = (c−b)q/(a−b) for mixing two goods to reach a target price

results.modern_name: Empirical study of primes in arithmetic progressions / prime races mod 8
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1837) for infinitude; Chebyshev (1853) for remarks on the bias between residue classes; Gauss is known for extensive prime counts (letter to Encke 1849)

deep.surprise_reason: The printed content is routine textbook commercial arithmetic. The marginalia show Gauss tabulating primes near 10^4 by residue class mod 8 and comparing class means. This fits his well-known habit of prime counting and tables. It is a small, interesting glimpse of empirical work on primes in progressions, but it is too fragmentary to show anything like a recognized Chebyshev-bias insight.
